problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/2ab398982e30d4b0ce633b77541596f3f5848e1b0a25539037ec3ee0fc557d4d.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point:  

$\,$ $x=-1.$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |

 

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical line $x=-1$ and choose an arbitrary point on it.

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/7719107149a10c6e5a22e6c343b532f3580582ebd78d3667aad5f2684d2f219d.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-1)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(-1,0)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-1.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=0$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0.$ So, the curve $y=f(x)$ is concave up on $(-\infty ,0).$ Also, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is constant and positive  to the right of $x=0$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ represents a section of an increasing straight line on $(0,\infty ).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/d81008f3d06f41f53a389fa2f36a7b12845fa3dae5a2707a739bbb500c8b4e56.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/763163652b41a7b3cc0b7a6b3faca4799cc073238a50afd9bd3d9c7767c32793.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
